title: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers
summary: Defines and discusses the requirements for devices that forward packets at the network layer of the Internet protocol suite, meaning IPv4 routers. It is a standards-track specification covering forwarding behavior and related protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1812 is a rulebook for machines that pass Internet packets along. It explains what IPv4 routers must do to check packets, choose where to send them, handle errors, talk to other routers, and be managed safely.

questions: what are the requirements for an ipv4 router
how should an ip router forward packets
how does a router choose the next hop
should a router forward directed broadcasts
what is router compliance in rfc 1812
subtitle: The rulebook that spells out what an IPv4 router must do to forward packets correctly.

tldr.problem: Routers from different vendors had to work together on the growing Internet, but the rules were scattered across many protocol documents and implementations made inconsistent choices.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1812 collects and clarifies the forwarding rules for IPv4 routers, stating requirements (MUST/SHOULD/MAY) for IP, ICMP, routing, management and operations.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 1009 and RFC 1716 as the router requirements document and has been updated by RFC 2644 and RFC 6633.

facts.label: Default TCP SendMSS
facts.value: 536 bytes if path MTU unknown; else path MTU minus 40 bytes

today: RFC 1812 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1009 and RFC 1716, and it has been updated by RFC 2644 and RFC 6633. It has not been obsoleted. It covers IP version 4 only.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1812 defines requirements for devices that perform the network layer forwarding function in the TCP/IP suite. The Internet community calls these devices IP routers (the OSI community calls them intermediate systems; older documents called them gateways).

A router differs from other packet switches because it examines the IP header and, typically, removes the link-layer header on receipt, modifies the IP header, and puts on a new link-layer header for retransmission.

The memo replaces RFC 1009 and RFC 1716 and covers only TCP/IP. It lists standard protocols a router must use, incorporates their specifications by reference, corrects errors in them, and adds guidance for implementers. The full requirements are mostly in the underlying protocol specifications, with RFC 1812 providing corrections and additions.

It should be read with the host requirements RFC 1122 and RFC 1123. The main difference is that routers implement forwarding algorithms; any host acting as a router must follow this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a rulebook for machines that pass Internet packets along. It says what IPv4 routers must do, and it fixes mistakes that appeared in earlier rulebooks.

sections.title: Reading Requirements and Compliance
sections.content:
The memo uses capitalized terms to rate requirements: MUST, MUST IMPLEMENT, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD IMPLEMENT, SHOULD NOT and MAY. MUST IMPLEMENT means the item must be built in, but need not be enabled by default.

Each major chapter has an introduction, a protocol walk-through (section by section through the referenced specifications), and a specific issues section. DISCUSSION and IMPLEMENTATION paragraphs explain and suggest; they are not part of the standard.

Compliance is only judged against requirements relevant to the features and protocols the router actually implements. Failure to meet any relevant MUST, MUST IMPLEMENT or MUST NOT means the implementation is not compliant.

A router may offer an option that violates a MUST only if the option's default setting conforms to the memo. The memo also notes it is closer to a profile than a full specification; implementors must still follow the underlying specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook uses special words to say how strict each rule is. 'MUST' means a rule you cannot skip, 'SHOULD' means a strong hint, and 'MAY' means it is up to you.

sections.title: Architecture and Assumptions
sections.content:
Chapter 2 gives background (no hard requirements). It lists what an Internet router does: implements IP/ICMP and required protocols; connects to two or more packet networks; receives and forwards datagrams while handling buffers, congestion and fairness; chooses a next hop from its routing database; runs interior gateway protocols and may run exterior ones; and provides management and support facilities.

Key architectural points: the Internet is a network of networks; routers keep no connection state (each packet is forwarded independently), so redundant paths survive failures while end-to-end flow control and reliability live in hosts; routing complexity belongs in routers, not hosts; and the system must tolerate wide variation in bandwidth, delay, loss, reordering and packet size.

Addressing: classical Class A to E prefixes are described as historical. CIDR replaces them with arbitrary-length network prefixes, built on topologically significant address assignment, routing protocols that aggregate reachability, and consistent longest-match forwarding. Routers SHOULD treat routes as network prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: A router is like a crossing with several roads. It looks at each packet's address, picks the next road, and does not remember the packet after that.

sections.title: IP Validation and Forwarding
sections.content:
Routers MUST implement IP, plus subnets, IP broadcast and CIDR. Before acting on any packet, a router MUST validate the header. A packet is silently discarded (and the error SHOULD be logged) if the link-layer length is less than the 20-byte minimum, the checksum is wrong, the IP version is not 4, the header length field is less than 5 words, or the total length cannot accommodate the header. These checks MUST NOT be disabled, and checksum verification MUST NOT be disabled.

Forwarding procedure: receive packet, validate header, process most options, then decide among three cases (packet is for the router itself, queued for forwarding, or forwarded and also delivered locally). For unicast, the forwarder finds the next hop, checks forwarding is permitted, decrements the TTL by at least one, finishes option processing, fragments if needed, finds the next hop's link-layer address, encapsulates and sends, and sends an ICMP Redirect if necessary.

Time to Live: A router MUST NOT check TTL except when forwarding. When forwarding it MUST reduce TTL by at least one. If TTL reaches zero the packet MUST be discarded, and for non-multicast destinations the router MUST send ICMP Time Exceeded code 0 (this is required because traceroute depends on it).

Fragmentation: A router MUST support fragmentation, SHOULD minimize the number of fragments, and MUST NOT reassemble a transit datagram before forwarding it (fragments may take different paths). Routers do reassemble datagrams addressed to themselves.

Reserved header bits MUST be ignored and passed through unchanged. Unrecognized IP options MUST be ignored and passed through unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: A router first checks that a packet's header is readable and sane. It then lowers a countdown number on the label. If the countdown hits zero, it throws the packet away and sends a note back.

sections.title: Choosing the Next Hop
sections.content:
To choose where to send a packet, the router first determines if the destination is directly reachable (by comparing network prefixes of its interfaces, and router-ids for unnumbered links). If not, it consults its Forwarding Information Base (FIB) and applies pruning rules in order until (usually) one route remains.

The required rules are Basic Match, Longest Match, Weak TOS (if TOS is considered), Best Metric and Vendor Policy. For example, for destination 10.144.2.5 with prefixes 10.144.2.0/24, 10.144.0.0/16, 10.0.0.0/8, Longest Match selects the /24. Preference runs from host routes, through network prefix routes of decreasing length, down to the default route (prefix length zero).

If no route remains, the packet MUST be discarded and an appropriate ICMP error generated. If several routes remain, the router may pick one arbitrarily or load-split; if it load-splits, the network manager SHOULD be able to disable it.

One suggested Vendor Policy is administrative preference, an integer from 0 (most preferred) to 254 (least preferred), with 255 meaning the route must never be used. The memo warns that misusing administrative preference can create routing loops.
sections.plainLanguage: The router has a list of possible roads. It crosses off roads that do not lead to the address, then picks the road that matches the address most closely.

sections.title: ICMP Errors and When Not to Send Them
sections.content:
Routers send ICMP to report forwarding problems. Equally important, they must stay quiet in certain cases. An ICMP error MUST NOT be sent in response to another ICMP error, a packet that fails header validation, a packet sent to an IP broadcast or multicast address or as a link-layer broadcast/multicast, a packet with an invalid source address, or any fragment other than the first. These restrictions take precedence over others and are intended to prevent broadcast storms.

Routers MUST be able to generate Destination Unreachable and SHOULD choose the code that best matches the cause. The memo defines codes 13, 14 and 15; code 6 SHOULD NOT be generated. Routers SHOULD limit the rate of ICMP errors and the rate limit parameters SHOULD be configurable.

Redirects: Routers MUST NOT generate network redirects (codes 0 and 2) and may only send host redirects. A redirect may only be sent when the packet leaves by the interface it arrived on, the source is on the same logical network as the next hop, and there is no source route option. A router running a routing protocol MUST NOT use paths learned from redirects.

Source Quench: Routers SHOULD NOT originate Source Quench messages.

Other behaviors include Echo server, responding to Address Mask Requests (configurable, default allows), and the router side of ICMP Router Discovery. Information Request/Reply are obsolete and SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router cannot deliver a packet it can send a note saying why. But it must never send notes about notes, or notes about broadcasts, or everyone would be buried in notes.

sections.title: Routing Protocols and Route Filtering
sections.content:
Interior routing (within an autonomous system) is separated from exterior routing (between systems). A router that implements any routing protocol other than static routes MUST IMPLEMENT OSPF (version 2 as referenced). Integrated IS-IS is also described. For exterior protocols, EGP is called historical; a router that implements EGP MUST IMPLEMENT BGP. RIP and EGP are covered in an appendix of historical protocols.

Routing is one place where the robustness principle does not apply; routers should be suspicious of routing data. They SHOULD rank information sources by trust, SHOULD filter obviously invalid routes (such as net 127), MUST NOT by default redistribute routes they do not use or trust, and SHOULD set IP precedence of routing traffic they originate to 6 (Internetwork Control).

Routers MUST support static routes, with each static route able to carry a metric for a given routing domain. They MUST be able to exchange routes between separate interior routing protocols, provide a mechanism to avoid loops when exchanging in both directions, and provide a way to prioritize routes from independent routing processes.

Route filtering requirements include accepting routing information on chosen logical interfaces and choosing whether all routes or only a default route is advertised on an interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers gossip with each other about which roads lead where. The rules say to trust good neighbors more, double-check strange gossip, and not pass along rumors you do not believe.

sections.title: Management, Configuration and Operations
sections.content:
Routers MUST be manageable by SNMP over UDP/IP, and all SNMP operations (get, get-next, get-response, set and trap) MUST be implemented. Management requests must work when sent to any IP address on any of the router's interfaces. Routers MUST rate-limit SNMP traps. The community table MUST allow at least one entry and SHOULD allow at least two, and be saved in non-volatile storage. If the community table starts with a default entry, it SHOULD be named public, be read-only, and MUST NOT send traps.

A router MUST implement standard MIBs appropriate to the interfaces and protocols it has (e.g. System, Interface, IP, ICMP, UDP groups of MIB-II; Interface Extensions MIB; IP Forwarding Table MIB). If it implements certain protocols (EGP, OSPF, BGP) it MUST implement their standard MIBs. Vendor-specific MIBs MUST expose everything not covered by standard ones.

Operations requirements: a router MUST NOT enable forwarding on an interface until it knows an IP address and mask/prefix length for it, or knows it is unnumbered with a router-id. Addresses/masks/prefixes MUST be explicitly configured (not factory defaults). Routers MUST support out-of-band access, MUST allow in-band and out-of-band reload, and SHOULD be reconfigurable without a reboot. A router SHOULD NOT believe protocols like RARP or ICMP Address Mask Reply for configuration.

In-band access MUST be provided, but for security it SHOULD be disabled by default, and the default must be documented. A router MUST be able to initiate an ICMP echo and SHOULD be able to initiate a traceroute.
sections.plainLanguage: The people who run the network need to check on routers from far away. So routers must answer questions, accept settings only from the right people, and never come with secret built-in passwords.

sections.title: Filtering, Broadcasts and Security
sections.content:
The memo focuses on interoperability but many rules affect security (denial of service, integrity, authentication). Few network protocols at the time had reasonable built-in security.

Address and source checks: Routers SHOULD NOT forward packets with invalid source or destination addresses (often called martians), or with addresses on network 0 or 127. Routers SHOULD IMPLEMENT source address validation (discard a packet whose arrival interface is not the one it would use to reach the source address), but this MUST be disabled by default because asymmetric paths can make it drop valid packets.

Broadcasts: Limited broadcasts MUST NOT be forwarded and MUST NOT be discarded. Network-prefix-directed broadcasts MUST be forwarded given a route and no policy, but a router MUST have an option to disable forwarding them, and MUST have an option to disable receiving them; both MUST default to permit. A router MUST NOT forward a packet it received as a link-layer broadcast unless it is directed to an IP multicast address. All-subnets-directed broadcasts are not meaningful under CIDR.

Filtering and options: Routers SHOULD offer packet filtering by source and destination prefix, with silent discard or ICMP code 13 reply. Source routing MUST be supported but may be disabled by an option that is not enabled by default. Record Route and Timestamp can reveal topology, so options to ignore them are allowed.

Auditing: Routers MUST provide a way to audit security failures and policy violations, limited or disabled on request, and MUST NOT have undocumented back doors or master passwords.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers have to be careful guards. They ignore packets with fake or impossible return addresses, do not repeat shouts meant for one street, and keep a log when someone tries something sneaky.

viz.caption: THE NEXT-HOP PRUNING RULES, APPLIED IN ORDER (RFC 1812)

items.title: 1. Basic Match
items.text: Keep only routes whose prefix matches the destination address.

items.title: 2. Longest Match
items.text: Of those, keep the routes with the longest prefix length.

items.title: 3. Weak TOS
items.text: Prefer routes whose TOS equals the packet's, else default TOS 0000. Applies only if TOS is considered.

items.title: 4. Best Metric
items.text: Within one routing domain, drop routes with an inferior metric.

items.title: 5. Vendor Policy
items.text: A catch-all for vendor-specific choices, such as administrative preference.

viz.caption: ICMP DESTINATION UNREACHABLE CODES DISCUSSED IN RFC 1812

items.label: Network Unreachable
items.desc: No route to the destination network.

items.label: Host Unreachable
items.desc: No path to a host on a directly connected network.

items.label: Fragmentation Needed and DF Set
items.desc: Fragmentation required but the DF flag is set.

items.label: Source Route Failed
items.desc: Cannot reach the next hop in a source route option.

items.label: Destination Network Unknown
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be generated; use code 0 instead.

items.label: Network Unreachable for TOS
items.desc: Routes exist but none has an acceptable TOS.

items.label: Host Unreachable for TOS
items.desc: No route matches the requested or default TOS.

items.label: Precedence Cutoff in Effect
items.desc: Packet precedence is below the minimum required.
